blocks: You Sent It Yourself.
One thousand, four hundred seventy-six dollars and eighty-nine cents. That is what one New Yorker sent through Zelle, to an account called Con Ed Billing.
The caller said his power would be shut off that same day. It was not the power company. And his bank told him it could not get that money back.
Why? Because he pressed send himself. Today: the scam, two lawsuits, and a rule that exists in Britain, but not in America.
Chapter one. The Shutoff.
Here is how New York's attorney general describes it. A caller claims to work for Con Edison, the utility. Pay your bill today, or the power goes off.
And the payment method is specific. Not a check. Not a card. Zelle, the transfer service built into the banking apps of millions of Americans.
The scammer used the name Con Ed Billing. On a small phone screen, that looks close enough to the real company.
He sent the money. Zelle says money typically reaches an enrolled recipient within minutes. And once that person is enrolled, the payment cannot be canceled.
That speed is the selling point. It is also the problem. By the time a victim realizes what happened, the money is usually gone.
The utility is just one costume. New York also describes scammers posing as banks, as government offices, and as sellers of things that do not exist.
And the scale is not small. In twenty twenty-four, Americans reported losing twelve and a half billion dollars to fraud. That is the FTC's count, up twenty-five percent in one year.
The FTC also found that people lost more money through bank transfers and cryptocurrency than through all other payment methods combined.
Zelle itself is enormous. By its own count, one trillion dollars moved across the network in twenty twenty-four.
When a network is that big, even a small share of bad payments means a lot of people, and a lot of money.
Chapter two. You Sent It Yourself.
So the man called his bank. According to New York, Chase told him it can't get that money back. To understand why, you need a law from nineteen seventy-eight.
The Electronic Fund Transfer Act, and the rule under it, called Regulation E. It protects you when money leaves your account without your permission.
Everything turns on one definition. An unauthorized transfer is one initiated by a person other than the consumer, without actual authority.
If a thief gets into your account and sends your money, that is unauthorized. Report it in time, and the bank must investigate, and your loss is capped.
But if a scammer talks you into pressing send yourself, you started that transfer. The definition was written for thieves, not for tricks.
And according to the CFPB, banks typically refuse to refund these tricked payments. The money left with your permission, even if the permission was based on a lie.
There is one exception, and Zelle wrote it. Since the middle of twenty twenty-three, the network has required refunds for some imposter scams.
But the CFPB called that a limited category, only a fraction of the fraud where people are tricked into paying. And it is the network's own policy. It is not a law.
So the victim carries the loss. Not because a court found the bank did something wrong, but because the law draws its line at who pressed the button.
Chapter three. Two Lawsuits.
December twentieth, twenty twenty-four. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued Zelle's operator, Early Warning Services, and three of the banks that own it.
JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo. Together, the CFPB said, those three handled seventy-three percent of the network's activity in twenty twenty-three.

The agency alleged that customers complained of fraud losses of over three hundred sixty million dollars at Chase, two hundred ninety million at Bank of America, and two hundred twenty million at Wells Fargo.
The director of the CFPB at the time, Rohit Chopra, announced the case. These were allegations, not findings.
And then the case was gone. On March fourth, twenty twenty-five, the CFPB dropped it. The next day, the judge dismissed it with prejudice, which means it cannot be filed again.
No court ever decided whether the banks did anything wrong. The federal case simply ended.
Five months later, New York picked it up. On August thirteenth, twenty twenty-five, Attorney General Letitia James sued Early Warning Services in state court.
Her office alleges that scammers took more than one billion dollars from Zelle users between twenty seventeen and twenty twenty-three.
The lawsuit claims Zelle launched without key safeguards. Sign-up lacked important verification steps, so scammers could hide behind misleading names. And transfers were immediate and irreversible.
It also alleges that the company developed basic safeguards as early as twenty nineteen, but failed to adopt them.
New York is asking for restitution and damages for New Yorkers, and a court order requiring Zelle to maintain anti-fraud measures.
Zelle has its side. In its own fact sheet, it says more than ninety-nine point nine five percent of its payments are completed with no report of fraud or scams.
So keep this straight. These are allegations. A lawsuit is not a verdict.
Chapter four. Across the Ocean.
Now look at Britain. There, this scam has an official name: authorized push payment fraud. You authorized the payment, but you were tricked into it.
On October seventh, twenty twenty-four, a new rule took effect. Banks must reimburse victims of these scams, up to eighty-five thousand pounds per claim.
The rule comes from a regulator, the Payment Systems Regulator. The victim's bank pays the refund, and the bank that received the money pays half of it back.
The deadline is five business days. Banks may keep an excess of up to one hundred pounds, but not from vulnerable customers.
There are limits. The rule does not cover a victim's own fraud, or gross negligence. And it does not cover international payments or crypto.
Did it work? In the first nine months, the regulator says, one hundred twelve million pounds went back to victims, from about one hundred twenty-six thousand claims.
Eighty-eight percent of the money claimed back was returned. A year earlier, the figure was sixty-six percent, although the regulator warns that its methods changed.
Same scam. Same button. In Britain, the line moved from who pressed send to who was tricked.
Chapter five. The Rule That Does Not Exist.
In America, someone tried. In August twenty twenty-four, Senators Richard Blumenthal and Elizabeth Warren introduced the Protecting Consumers From Payment Scams Act.
Its goal, in its own words: to treat fraudulently induced transfers in the same manner as unauthorized ones. In other words, to close the gap.
It did not become law.
So today, the American rule is still the one from nineteen seventy-eight. If you pressed send, your refund depends on your bank, and on Zelle's own policy.
New York's lawsuit may change how Zelle works. But a lawsuit against one company is not a rule for everyone.
Chapter six. Before You Press Send.
First, the lesson from New York. A same-day threat plus a demand to pay by Zelle is the pattern. Treat it as a red flag.
Hang up. Call back using the number on your bill, on your card, or on the company's official website. Never the number the caller gives you.
Zelle's own advice is to only send money to people you know and trust. A utility bill is not that.
And read the name on the screen before you send. In the New York case, one made-up name did all the work.
If it already happened, call your bank right away. Ask whether your case qualifies under Zelle's imposter scam policy, and put your dispute in writing.
Then report it. To the FTC at reportfraud dot ftc dot gov. To the FBI at I C three dot gov. And if your bank says no, go to consumerfinance dot gov slash complaint.
If you live in New York, the attorney general's Consumer Frauds Bureau also takes reports.
One thousand, four hundred seventy-six dollars and eighty-nine cents. One fake name. One press of a button.
In Britain, that press of a button is no longer the end of the story. In America, for now, it still is.
Which scam should we investigate next? Tell me in the comments. And subscribe to The Rule Changed, for the scam, the case, and the rule.
